items.prompt: A company wants different encryption, access, retention, and recovery controls for public, internal, confidential, and regulated data. What should the architect establish first?
constraints: Data has different business and regulatory impact.
Controls must be repeatable across accounts.
The classification must drive enforceable decisions rather than labels only.

options.text: Define a data-classification taxonomy with owners, handling requirements, retention rules, access expectations, and evidence for each class.
Classify all data as confidential because one label is simpler and makes every workload compliant automatically.
Use AWS Region names as the classification because geographic placement alone determines sensitivity.
Rely on storage-class names because S3 and database storage classes automatically encode business sensitivity.

feedback.Reason: Classification is useful only when it maps data sensitivity to owners and concrete controls across its lifecycle.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A taxonomy gives architects and operators a shared way to identify handling, access, encryption, retention, backup, and evidence requirements. AWS services enforce parts of the model but do not infer the business class automatically.
Details.scenarioApplication: The governance team defines classes, assigns data owners, maps each class to S3, database, key, backup, and deletion controls, and tests the mappings.
Details.errorCorrection: One label does not create compliance, Region and storage class are technical attributes rather than complete sensitivity classifications, and labels without controls are metadata-only avoidance.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A richer taxonomy improves precision but requires training, metadata quality, and ongoing owner review.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A single broad label does not define proportional controls or prove that every workload is compliant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Region can affect residency but does not by itself describe business sensitivity or handling requirements.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Storage classes optimize storage behavior and do not encode the organization’s complete data sensitivity model.

items.prompt: A compliance team cannot identify which S3 buckets contain personal data because data owners rely on object names alone. Which discovery approach is appropriate?
constraints: Sensitive values may appear in arbitrary object names.
The estate contains many buckets and accounts.
The team needs evidence that coverage is not based only on naming conventions.

options.text: Use supported sensitive-data discovery such as Macie, combine content findings with bucket and object metadata, and record scope and coverage limits.
Search only bucket names because object names always identify their complete data contents.
Use IAM policy names because authorization policy text contains every sensitive value stored in S3.
Assume encryption metadata identifies personal data because every encrypted object contains regulated information.

feedback.Reason: Sensitive-data discovery needs content-aware analysis and inventory context; names, policies, and encryption state are insufficient proxies.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Macie can analyze supported S3 data with managed or custom identifiers, while inventory and ownership metadata provide location and scope context. Discovery results still require review and coverage accounting.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team scans high-value buckets, maps findings to owners, records excluded or sampled data, and updates the classification register.
Details.errorCorrection: Object names can be misleading, IAM policy text does not contain stored values, and encryption is a protection state rather than a sensitivity classification.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Content discovery improves confidence but introduces processing cost, access planning, false positives, and residual coverage considerations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Bucket and object names are metadata and cannot establish the sensitivity of arbitrary contents.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM policies describe permissions and do not enumerate values inside S3 objects.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Encryption can apply to public or internal data and does not prove a regulated classification.

items.prompt: A data-governance program needs to locate sensitive data in S3, assign findings to data owners, and feed the classification register. Which use of Macie is appropriate?
constraints: The program is about data discovery and governance.
S3 buckets span multiple teams.
Findings require owner review before classification changes.

options.text: Use Macie to discover sensitive data and S3 policy conditions, then route findings to data owners and record reviewed classifications and scope.
Use Macie as the sole authorization layer because a discovery finding automatically changes every S3 bucket policy.
Use GuardDuty instead because threat findings automatically classify all S3 object contents for governance.
Use CloudTrail management events alone because API activity logs contain the complete content classification of every object.

feedback.Reason: Macie supplies discovery and findings; governance owners still review classifications and implement access or lifecycle controls separately.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Macie reports sensitive-data and S3 policy findings. It does not automatically set business ownership, change every bucket policy, or replace access governance.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security team sends Macie findings to the appropriate data owner, records the decision, and opens remediation for policy or lifecycle gaps.
Details.errorCorrection: A finding does not grant or revoke S3 access, GuardDuty is a threat detector rather than a content classifier, and CloudTrail activity is not object-content classification.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Macie improves discovery coverage but needs governance workflow, owner decisions, and explicit control changes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Macie findings inform governance but do not automatically replace S3 authorization policies.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: GuardDuty detects suspicious activity and does not classify every S3 object’s contents.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CloudTrail records API activity and identity, not a complete classification of object content.

items.prompt: A platform team needs a recurring inventory of S3 objects, including keys, sizes, versions, encryption status, and storage class, before applying governance rules. Which S3 feature is a fit?
constraints: The team needs object metadata at scale.
The inventory can be delivered to a destination bucket.
The inventory is not itself content classification.

options.text: Configure S3 Inventory for the required bucket and object metadata, then use the inventory as an input to lifecycle, compliance, and discovery workflows.
Use a security group because it records object size and storage class for each S3 request.
Use an IAM policy document because it enumerates every object version and its encryption status automatically.
Use CloudFront cache statistics because edge metrics are the authoritative inventory of all bucket objects and versions.

feedback.Reason: S3 Inventory produces scheduled object metadata reports that can support governance and lifecycle analysis at scale.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Inventory reports can include object metadata such as size, storage class, encryption, and version information according to the configured scope. They do not inspect arbitrary object content.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform delivers reports to a protected destination, uses them to find unclassified or stale objects, and combines them with Macie or owner review for content sensitivity.
Details.errorCorrection: Security groups are network controls, IAM policies describe authorization, and CloudFront metrics do not represent the complete bucket object inventory.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Inventory is efficient for metadata governance but may be periodic and must be protected as a data-management artifact.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Security groups do not record S3 object metadata or storage class.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM policy documents do not enumerate every object version and its encryption state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CloudFront cache metrics cover delivery behavior, not the authoritative contents of an S3 bucket.

items.prompt: A data owner wants to mark S3 objects with a classification and use the tag in access or lifecycle workflows. Which design is appropriate?
constraints: The classification is metadata assigned by an owner or workflow.
Tags must not be treated as proof of content when no discovery has occurred.
Policies must support the chosen tag conditions.

options.text: Use S3 object tags as governed metadata, restrict who can set or change them, and combine tag conditions with discovery and resource-policy controls.
Allow every writer to change the classification tag because object tags cannot affect lifecycle or authorization decisions.
Use the object filename as the immutable classification because tags are not retained with object versions.
Encrypt the tag with a KMS key and assume the encryption key proves the tag is accurate without owner review.

feedback.Reason: Object tags can drive governance workflows, but their integrity and ownership must be controlled; a tag is metadata, not automatic proof of content sensitivity.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: S3 object tags are key-value metadata that can be used by supported policies and lifecycle configurations. Unauthorized tag changes can undermine tag-based governance.
Details.scenarioApplication: The data-governance workflow sets tags after review, restricts TagObject and DeleteObjectTagging, and tests that access and lifecycle behavior follows the approved values.
Details.errorCorrection: Writers may need to be restricted from changing classification, filenames are not immutable classifications, and encryption protects tag data but does not validate its truth.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Tags are flexible and inexpensive governance metadata but require integrity controls, versioning decisions, and remediation for untagged objects.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: If tags drive governance, unrestricted tag changes let writers bypass the intended classification controls.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Filenames are mutable metadata and do not provide the same governed object-tag behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Encrypting a tag protects it from disclosure but does not prove the classification is correct.

items.prompt: Analytics teams need a searchable inventory of datasets, schemas, locations, and ownership without granting every analyst raw access to every object. Which AWS capability should be evaluated?
constraints: The team needs metadata discovery.
Raw data access must remain governed.
The catalog must be connected to data owners and policies.

options.text: Use a governed data catalog such as the AWS Glue Data Catalog for dataset metadata, then enforce raw-data access separately with IAM, Lake Formation, and service policies.
Make every S3 bucket public so analysts can discover schemas without authorization or catalog maintenance.
Use CloudTrail as the data catalog because API event history automatically stores schema and ownership for every dataset.
Use a KMS key alias as the dataset schema because key names are the authoritative data dictionary.

feedback.Reason: A data catalog provides searchable metadata, while data-access governance remains a separate control plane.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The Glue Data Catalog stores metadata about data locations and schemas for supported analytics workflows. Catalog visibility does not automatically grant permission to read the underlying data.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform registers datasets, assigns owners and classifications, and uses Lake Formation or IAM policies to grant only approved columns, tables, or locations.
Details.errorCorrection: Public buckets expose data, CloudTrail is an audit log rather than a schema catalog, and KMS aliases are not data dictionaries.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Central metadata improves discoverability but requires catalog freshness, ownership, and access-policy integration.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Public storage is not a safe substitute for metadata discovery or access governance.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: CloudTrail records API activity and does not automatically provide complete dataset schema and ownership metadata.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: KMS aliases identify keys and do not describe dataset schemas or business ownership.

items.prompt: A data lake needs centralized permissions for databases, tables, columns, and governed cross-account sharing. Which AWS service should the architect evaluate?
constraints: The lake uses supported AWS analytics services.
Access must be granted by data resource rather than broad bucket access.
The security team owns governance while data teams own datasets.

options.text: Evaluate AWS Lake Formation for centralized data-lake permissions and governance, while preserving underlying S3, catalog, and IAM prerequisites.
Use a security group because it can grant column-level access to S3-backed tables.
Use a KMS key policy alone because encryption keys automatically express every table and column permission.
Use CloudFront because CDN distributions provide centralized data-lake column filtering for analysts.

feedback.Reason: Lake Formation is designed to govern access to data-lake resources such as databases, tables, and columns for supported analytics workflows.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Lake Formation integrates with the Glue Data Catalog and supported services to express fine-grained data permissions. S3 locations, IAM, roles, and trusted-resource configuration still form part of the access path.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security team registers data locations, grants analysts approved table or column access, and verifies that raw bucket access cannot bypass the governance model.
Details.errorCorrection: Security groups are network controls, KMS policies protect key operations rather than table permissions, and CloudFront does not provide data-lake authorization.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Centralized governance improves consistency but requires migration of existing permissions and careful handling of direct S3 access paths.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Security groups control network reachability and do not grant table or column permissions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: KMS key policies authorize cryptographic operations and cannot express all data-lake table or column access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CloudFront delivers content and does not govern analyst access to data-lake tables or columns.

items.prompt: A classification scheme has labels but no mapping from 'regulated' to encryption, retention, access, backup, and evidence requirements. What is missing?
constraints: The labels must affect architecture decisions.
Multiple teams implement the controls.
The governance program needs repeatable review evidence.

options.text: Add a control matrix that maps each class to approved storage, access, encryption, retention, backup, deletion, and evidence requirements with named owners.
Add more labels without control mappings because a larger taxonomy automatically enforces handling requirements.
Rename the classes after AWS services because service names are sufficient policy definitions.
Hide the unimplemented classes from the catalog so the taxonomy appears complete to auditors.

feedback.Reason: A classification taxonomy becomes operational through explicit control mappings and ownership, not through labels or presentation alone.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The matrix connects business sensitivity to technical and process controls. Owners can then select AWS services and validate evidence against a known requirement set.
Details.scenarioApplication: The governance team maps regulated data to KMS, Lake Formation, backup, Object Lock, retention, and audit controls and assigns review responsibility.
Details.errorCorrection: More labels without controls increase metadata without improving protection, service names are not policies, and hiding gaps creates false assurance.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A small actionable taxonomy is better than an unowned label set, but each class must remain meaningful and maintained.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Additional labels do not enforce handling requirements without mapped controls and owners.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: AWS service names do not define business sensitivity or complete policy requirements.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Hiding a missing mapping would create false assurance rather than fix the governance gap.

items.prompt: A discovery finding identifies customer data in a bucket, but no team knows who can approve access, retention, or deletion. Which governance control is missing?
constraints: The bucket is used by multiple applications.
Security can detect the data but cannot make business decisions alone.
Access and retention approvals must be accountable.

options.text: Assign a data owner and steward for the dataset, record the owner with the classification metadata, and require owner approval for access and lifecycle decisions.
Assign ownership to the S3 bucket name because object storage automatically determines the business owner.
Let the security team approve every business use permanently because detection findings replace data ownership.
Delete the bucket to remove the need for a data owner or retention decision.

feedback.Reason: Data ownership connects technical discovery to accountable decisions about access, retention, classification, and deletion.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A data owner understands the business purpose and approves handling requirements; a steward or platform team can implement controls and evidence. AWS metadata can record ownership, but the organization must define the role.
Details.scenarioApplication: The governance register links the dataset to an owner, class, approved consumers, retention, backup, and deletion process.
Details.errorCorrection: Bucket names do not determine business ownership, security detection does not replace owner approval, and deletion without governance can violate retention or recovery needs.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Named ownership improves accountability but requires organizational agreement when data crosses teams or accounts.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A bucket is a technical container and does not automatically identify the business owner.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security teams can provide control expertise but should not replace business ownership for legitimate use and retention decisions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deletion without owner and retention review can destroy required data or evidence.

items.prompt: A team proposes using an S3 tag 'public' as proof that an object contains no personal data. What should the review conclude?
constraints: The tag is set by an upload workflow.
Object content is not inspected consistently.
A false classification could create disclosure risk.

options.text: Treat the tag as governed metadata, not conclusive content evidence; combine owner attestation or content discovery with controls that prevent unauthorized tag changes.
Accept the tag as definitive because S3 tags are cryptographically guaranteed to describe every byte in the object.
Remove encryption because the tag already proves the object is public and non-sensitive.
Use a DNS TXT record with the same value because DNS metadata validates S3 object contents.

feedback.Reason: Metadata is useful for routing and policy but does not automatically establish the truth of the underlying data content.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: S3 tags are separate object metadata and can be changed by authorized actions. Content-aware discovery or accountable owner review is needed when the classification has high consequence.
Details.scenarioApplication: The governance workflow restricts tag writes, samples or scans content, records owner decisions, and denies public exposure until the classification is supported.
Details.errorCorrection: Tags are not cryptographic content proofs, encryption should not be removed, and DNS records do not validate object contents.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Content discovery costs more than metadata-only classification but reduces the risk of a dangerous false label.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: S3 tags are metadata and can be incorrect or changed; they do not describe every byte cryptographically.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A classification label does not remove the need for encryption or access protection.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS metadata has no authoritative relationship to the contents of an S3 object.

items.prompt: A discovery job covers only production buckets and excludes development accounts, but the compliance report says 'all company data classified.' What should the architect change?
constraints: The job scope is intentionally limited.
Development data may still contain copied production records.
The report must match actual coverage.

options.text: State the covered accounts, buckets, objects, and exclusions explicitly, classify the excluded scope as a residual risk, and expand discovery or obtain an approved exception.
Keep the report unchanged because a production-only scan proves that development data is non-sensitive by definition.
Delete development accounts from the inventory so the report becomes accurate without additional discovery.
Assume encryption in development makes discovery unnecessary because encrypted data cannot contain regulated values.

feedback.Reason: Discovery evidence must state its scope and exclusions; an unscanned area cannot be represented as classified without an approved basis.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Macie jobs, inventory, and catalog workflows have explicit account, Region, bucket, prefix, object, and sampling boundaries. Governance reports should preserve those boundaries and residual risk.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team inventories development copies, expands the job where required, or records a time-bound exception with an owner and remediation date.
Details.errorCorrection: Development data can contain sensitive copies, deleting inventory hides a gap, and encryption protects content without classifying it.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Broader discovery costs more but supports a truthful compliance claim; exclusions require risk acceptance rather than metadata labels.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Environment name does not prove that copied data is non-sensitive.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Removing an account from the inventory hides the scope gap instead of solving it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Encryption does not make data classification unnecessary.

items.prompt: A security account must discover sensitive data in member-account S3 buckets while application accounts retain ownership of remediation. Which governance pattern is appropriate?
constraints: The accounts belong to one AWS Organization.
The security account is an approved delegated administrator.
Member buckets require explicit coverage and owner routing.

options.text: Configure the supported organization-level Macie administration and member-account coverage, then route findings to each data owner and monitor Regional scope.
Use the management account root user to read every member bucket directly because delegated administration cannot cover data discovery.
Share all member bucket objects publicly with the security account because cross-account discovery requires public reads.
Use AWS WAF because a web ACL can inspect every object in member-account S3 buckets without account configuration.

feedback.Reason: Macie supports organization-oriented administration, but member-account and Regional coverage, permissions, and finding ownership remain explicit.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: An organization administrator configures Macie and member accounts according to the service model. Data owners remain responsible for decisions about access, remediation, and retention on their resources.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security account enables required Regions, verifies member status, and assigns Macie findings to the account and data owners without using routine root operations.
Details.errorCorrection: Root use is unsafe, public bucket access is not required, and WAF does not inspect S3 content for classification.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Central administration improves coverage consistency but requires account lifecycle, Region, permissions, and owner coordination.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Organization administration exists to avoid routine management-account root operations and still requires explicit coverage setup.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Public exposure is unnecessary and would create a serious data disclosure risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: WAF protects web requests and is not a cross-account S3 content-discovery service.

items.prompt: Macie finds a string that matches a managed identifier in a public documentation example, but the data owner confirms it is not a live credential. How should governance handle the result?
constraints: The finding is not automatically invalid.
The owner can provide business context.
The team wants to reduce repeated noise without hiding real matches.

options.text: Validate the object and context, document the owner decision, use a narrow allow list or identifier adjustment where appropriate, and retest nearby real values.
Delete every finding of that identifier type because one documentation example proves the pattern is always a false positive.
Publish the finding publicly so other teams can decide whether the matched value is sensitive.
Disable encryption for the object because a false positive means the object contains no data risk.

feedback.Reason: False-positive handling needs scoped evidence and owner review; a local exception must not erase detection for unrelated data.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Macie allow lists and identifier configuration can reduce known noise, but the pattern and scope affect future findings. Governance retains the decision and tests the control.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team records the object, owner, pattern, expiration or review condition, and validation evidence before changing discovery configuration.
Details.errorCorrection: Deleting all findings creates blind spots, public disclosure exposes security data, and encryption is independent of classification accuracy.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Noise reduction improves operations but must be narrower than the population of real sensitive values.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A single false positive does not justify suppressing all findings for the identifier type.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Findings may contain sensitive resource and data context and should not be published publicly.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A false positive does not imply that encryption should be removed or that all data risk is absent.

items.prompt: A residency review must identify every Region and account where customer records or derived exports exist. Which inventory design is most defensible?
constraints: Data is copied by backup, analytics, and application workflows.
The inventory must include copies and derived exports.
Region is one attribute, not the complete classification.

options.text: Maintain an authoritative data-location register fed by resource inventory, backup and replication configuration, S3 inventory, catalog metadata, and owner attestations.
Inspect only primary database Regions because backups and exports inherit residency automatically without separate records.
Use IAM policy Region conditions as the complete data inventory because denied Regions cannot contain data.
Use the AWS account name as the location record because account names encode every Region used by its resources.

feedback.Reason: Residency evidence must account for primary data, backups, replicas, logs, and derived copies across accounts and Regions.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: AWS resources and data copies have service-specific Regional and replication behavior. Inventory, backup, replication, and catalog signals must be reconciled with owner knowledge.
Details.scenarioApplication: The governance team records the source, copy type, Region, account, classification, retention, encryption key, and deletion owner for each data location.
Details.errorCorrection: Backups and exports do not automatically disappear from residency analysis, IAM conditions are authorization not inventory, and account names do not enumerate resources.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A complete register requires ongoing integration and reconciliation but supports residency, recovery, and deletion decisions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Backups, replicas, logs, and exports can be separate data locations with their own Region and retention behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM conditions restrict requests but do not prove which resources or copies exist.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Account names are labels and do not enumerate Regions or resource data locations.

items.prompt: A data owner wants to know which principals can read a confidential S3 dataset, including access granted through bucket policy, access points, and roles. Which review is needed?
constraints: The dataset has multiple policy paths.
The owner needs effective access, not only a list of users.
The review must include cross-account principals.

options.text: Analyze identity policies, bucket and access-point policies, role trust, Organizations controls, endpoint policies, and CloudTrail access evidence to determine effective and observed access.
List IAM users only because roles, resource policies, and service principals cannot read S3 data.
Read the S3 object names because names reveal every principal that has accessed the data.
Use KMS key rotation history as the complete access report because every S3 read is a key-management event owned by KMS.

feedback.Reason: Effective data access is the result of multiple policy layers, while CloudTrail provides observed use rather than proving every theoretical permission.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: S3 authorization can involve identity, resource, access-point, endpoint, SCP, session, and KMS policies. CloudTrail data events can show observed object access when configured.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team computes policy reach, reviews role trust and cross-account paths, and compares the result with logged reads to find unused or unexpected access.
Details.errorCorrection: IAM users are only one principal type, object names do not record access, and KMS rotation history is not an S3 access log.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Effective-access review is complex but necessary for confidential data; observed logs and policy analysis answer different questions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Roles, resource policies, access points, services, and cross-account principals can all participate in S3 access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Object names do not identify authorized or observed principals.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: KMS key lifecycle events do not provide a complete record of S3 object reads.

items.prompt: An auditor asks why a dataset is classified as regulated and whether the discovery covered all copies. What evidence should the program retain?
constraints: The classification has a named owner.
Discovery scope changes over time.
Evidence must not expose raw sensitive values unnecessarily.

options.text: Retain the classification decision, owner approval, discovery method and scope, findings summary, exceptions, data-location register, and control evidence without storing unnecessary plaintext sensitive content.
Retain only one sample plaintext record because it proves every copy has the same classification.
Delete discovery reports after the classification label is set because labels are permanent evidence by themselves.
Publish all findings to a public dashboard so auditors can independently inspect the raw data and scope.

feedback.Reason: Classification evidence should establish decision, owner, method, scope, exceptions, and controls while minimizing exposure of sensitive values.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A governed evidence record links discovery output to a data owner and control implementation. Scope and exceptions show what was and was not examined at the time.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team stores protected reports and metadata, records the job or inventory configuration, and provides auditors controlled access to evidence rather than raw customer data.
Details.errorCorrection: One sample cannot prove all copies, deleting reports removes scope evidence, and public dashboards can disclose sensitive findings.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Protected evidence has storage and access costs but supports auditability and future reclassification.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A sample record cannot establish classification or coverage for every copy and may create unnecessary sensitive-data exposure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The label alone does not preserve the discovery scope, owner decision, or exception history.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Audit access should be controlled and should not require public disclosure of raw security findings or data.

items.prompt: Which pairing best matches the discovery need?
constraints: The architect must choose services by evidence type.
The data is in different AWS stores.
The team must not claim that one service answers every governance question.

options.text: Use Macie for supported S3 sensitive-data discovery, S3 Inventory or a catalog for metadata, CloudTrail for observed access, and Lake Formation for governed data-lake permissions where supported.
Use GuardDuty for all content classification, IAM for object inventory, and WAF for data-lake permissions because security services are interchangeable.
Use KMS for content discovery, CloudFront for access governance, and Route 53 for backup location because each service is global.
Use only S3 object names because adding multiple evidence sources makes classification impossible to audit.

feedback.Reason: Data governance combines different evidence types, so the architecture should assign each question to the service that actually answers it.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Macie analyzes supported S3 content, Inventory and catalogs describe data locations and schemas, CloudTrail records observed API activity, and Lake Formation governs supported data-lake resources.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect builds a governance evidence pipeline that preserves source context and avoids treating a discovery finding as an authorization decision.
Details.errorCorrection: GuardDuty, IAM, WAF, KMS, CloudFront, and Route 53 have different service boundaries and cannot be substituted for the listed governance functions.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Multiple signals require correlation and ownership but produce a more defensible classification and access picture.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Those services do not provide the listed content, inventory, and data-lake governance functions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The services listed have different purposes and do not become governance tools merely because they are AWS services.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Names alone cannot establish content sensitivity, access, location, or evidence coverage.

items.prompt: A new data platform has no inventory, owner register, discovery schedule, classification metadata, or evidence retention. Which first slice creates a coherent governance baseline?
constraints: The platform will grow across accounts and Regions.
The baseline must be implementable now.
The team must expose gaps rather than mark them complete without evidence.

options.text: Create an authoritative data register with owners and locations, define actionable classes, enable metadata inventory and sensitive-data discovery for priority scope, and retain protected evidence with explicit exclusions.
Add a 'compliant' tag to every resource and defer discovery because metadata labels are sufficient for the initial launch.
Make all data public temporarily so teams can discover it before governance controls are designed.
Delete unclassified datasets because unknown classification is proof that they have no approved business purpose.

feedback.Reason: A coherent baseline establishes owners, locations, actionable classes, discovery evidence, and explicit coverage limits instead of pretending labels or deletion solve unknowns.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Governance begins with inventory and accountability, then applies discovery and control mappings to prioritized data. Scope and exceptions remain visible until addressed.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform team registers datasets, assigns owners, runs Macie or equivalent discovery for high-risk S3 data, catalogs metadata, and reports uncovered scope.
Details.errorCorrection: A compliance tag without evidence is not a control, public exposure is unsafe, and deleting unknown data may violate retention or business requirements.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Prioritization makes the baseline achievable, but excluded data must be visible with an owner and a plan rather than silently omitted.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A label without inventory, discovery, owner, and evidence does not establish compliance.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Public exposure is a security failure and is not a discovery method.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Unknown classification is not proof that data may be deleted; retention and owner decisions are required.
